title: Early modern philosophy II: the empiricists and Kant
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Read Locke, Berkeley and Hume on ideas, substance, primary and secondary qualities, personal identity, causation, induction and the self, Reid's common-sense reply, and Kant's Critique of Pure Reason on synthetic a priori knowledge, space and time, the categories and the limits of metaphysics.
primary_reading: Early Modern Texts: free modernized versions of the classic texts

weeks.1: Locke: ideas and the rejection of innate ideas
weeks.2: Locke: substance and primary and secondary qualities
weeks.4: Berkeley: to be is to be perceived
weeks.5: Berkeley: God, laws of nature and the objection from science
weeks.6: Hume: impressions, ideas and the copy principle
weeks.9: Hume: the self, skepticism and natural belief
weeks.10: Reid: common sense and the reply to Hume
weeks.11: Kant: synthetic a priori judgments, space and time
weeks.12: Kant: the categories, the antinomies and the limits of metaphysics

blocks.deliverable: Sort ten qualities into primary and secondary and explain why.
Reconstruct Locke's memory criterion and one objection.
Reconstruct Berkeley's master argument and evaluate it.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct the problem of induction.
Compare Hume's bundle view of the self with Reid's reply.
Explain one antinomy and Kant's resolution.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Causation from Hume to Kant: write a 2,000-word essay that reconstructs Hume's account of causation and his problem of induction, explains how Kant answers Hume, and evaluates whether Kant's answer succeeds, using passages from the modernized texts.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
